COLDWAR_SOV_pod_republic_councils: Every union republic already has its own Council of Ministers, yet in practice these governments wait on orders from the all-Union ministries in Moscow. Podgorny, who ran Ukraine before coming to the Kremlin, knows how little room the republics truly have. Giving their governments real authority over local industry and services would bind the republics more firmly to the Union, even if it adds another layer of officials to pay.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_republican_accounting: Under khozraschet, Soviet enterprises are supposed to balance their own books, but the republics themselves still live on allocations handed down by Gosplan. Letting each republic keep part of what it earns and answer for its own costs would reward the efficient and expose the wasteful. Kiev, Minsk and Tbilisi would gain a stake in their own prosperity, and the Union a reason to trust them.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_soviet_of_nationalit: The Supreme Soviet has two chambers, and the Soviet of Nationalities was meant to give every republic and autonomous region an equal voice. For decades it has done little more than applaud. As Chairman of the Presidium, Podgorny can breathe life into it, letting deputies from Tashkent to Tallinn debate the questions that touch their peoples and turning a ceremonial body into a genuine forum of the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_strong_presidium: Under the Constitution the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet is the collective head of the Soviet state, yet real power has always rested with the Party. Podgorny intends to change that balance. A Presidium that drafts decrees, oversees ministries and speaks for the state would govern more efficiently, but the Party apparatus and the republican leaders will not surrender their prerogatives quietly.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_ministers_answer_to_the_: The branch ministries have grown into fiefdoms that answer to Central Committee secretaries and defend their own plans at any cost. If ministers were made accountable to the Presidium and the Council of Ministers rather than to Party patrons, orders could flow through a single chain of command. The industrial ministries would welcome clearer authority, and the planners hope for fewer contradictory instructions.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_presidential_decrees: Between sessions of the Supreme Soviet, the Presidium governs through decrees, the ukazy that carry Podgorny's signature. Used boldly, this instrument can settle questions the Politburo prefers to postpone, from pensions to the rights of the republics. Every decree published in Izvestia reminds the country that the Soviet state has a head of its own, and that his word is law.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_state_security_counc: Questions of internal security are settled in closed meetings between the KGB chairman and the General Secretary. A State Security Council attached to the Presidium would bring defence, internal affairs and state security together under the head of state. The Lubyanka gains a seat at the highest table of government, while the state gains a firmer grip on the guardians of its ideological order.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_head_of_state_diplomacy: As formal head of state, Podgorny receives ambassadors, signs treaties and travels where the General Secretary cannot. A grand tour of Africa and the Middle East, like the journey that historically took him to Tanzania, Zambia, Mozambique and Somalia in 1977, would give Moscow a dignified and personal face in Cairo, Damascus, Addis Ababa and Luanda.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_treaty_signer: Treaties of friendship are the currency of Soviet influence in the Third World, and the head of state is the natural man to sign them. Historically, it was Podgorny who flew to Cairo in May 1971 to sign the first such pact with an Arab state. Making him the Union's treaty signer would let Moscow bind Egypt, Iraq and India more quickly and present the socialist community as a reliable partner.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_ukrainian_breadbasket: The black earth of Ukraine still feeds much of the Union, but its kolkhozes suffer from poor machinery, wasted harvests and low procurement prices. Podgorny, once First Secretary in Kiev, understands the republic's countryside better than anyone in the Politburo. Investment in fertiliser, irrigation and storage could restore Ukraine's role as the breadbasket of the Union and win the loyalty of its villages.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_donbass_coal: The mines of the Donets Basin powered the first Five-Year Plans and remain the heart of Ukrainian heavy industry. Yet the shafts are deep, the seams are thinning and the miners are growing restless. New power stations and modernised pits would keep the furnaces of the south burning, and a government that looks after the miners can count on the support of the trade unions.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_final_form: Podgorny's reforms have raised a question the Party has long avoided: what kind of state should the Soviet Union ultimately be? One path leads to a looser union in which the republics stand as sovereign partners. The other leads to a strong Soviet presidency that rules above the Party apparatus. The choice will define the Union for a generation.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_union_of_sovereign_state: What if the Union were refounded as a voluntary association of sovereign republics, bound by treaty rather than by the will of the Central Committee? Pyotr Shelest, Kiev's outspoken defender of Ukrainian interests, would lead the new union as its first head. The republics would welcome the change, yet abandoning the leading role of the Communist Party will shake the foundations of the old order.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_soviet_presidency: Foreign newspapers already call Podgorny the Soviet President, though no such office exists. Turning the chairmanship of the Presidium into a true presidency, with its own staff and powers, would give the state a head who does not depend on the goodwill of the Party apparatus. The General Secretary would remain influential, but no longer the only master in the Kremlin.
COLDWAR_SOV_pod_the_soviet_state: The state has finally stepped out of the shadow of the Party. Ministries answer to the government, the republics have their voice in the Supreme Soviet, and the head of state speaks with real authority at home and abroad. Podgorny's vision of a Soviet Union governed by its own institutions has become reality, and the system looks steadier than it has in decades.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_grey_cardinal_rules: For decades Mikhail Suslov has guarded the purity of the Party line from the shadows, shaping every major speech, textbook and Pravda editorial. Now the Grey Cardinal stands at the head of the Party itself. Ascetic, cautious and unyielding, he intends to defend Marxism-Leninism against revisionism at home and abroad, even if innovation and scientific freedom must pay the price.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_ideological_commissi: Ideological work is scattered among the propaganda, culture and science departments of the Central Committee, each guarding its own turf. Suslov proposes a single commission to coordinate them all, from university lecture halls to factory wall newspapers. With one hand on every lever of propaganda, the Party can renew the faith of its members and remind the nomenklatura where their loyalty belongs.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_ponomarevs_department: Boris Ponomarev has run the International Department of the Central Committee since 1955, maintaining Moscow's ties with communist parties and liberation movements across the globe. Under Suslov's protection, the department can expand its funding, its party schools and its network of contacts in Havana, Hanoi and Ulan Bator. The socialist community needs a guiding centre, and Ponomarev is eager to provide it.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_trapeznikovs_science_dep: Sergei Trapeznikov, head of the Central Committee's Department of Science and Educational Institutions, is an old companion of Brezhnev and an open admirer of Stalin. Under his supervision, academic appointments and research topics are screened for ideological reliability. Scholars at the Academy of Sciences grumble about lost freedom, but the neo-Stalinist wing of the Party sees in him a champion of discipline in the institutes.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_line: Every communist knows that the Party line must be followed, but where exactly does it run? Suslov must decide whether to concentrate on guarding the ideological purity of Soviet society at home, or to carry the struggle against imperialism and revisionism abroad. Both paths lead back to Marxism-Leninism, yet they demand very different resources and face very different enemies.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_ideological_purity: Samizdat manuscripts pass from hand to hand, foreign radio stations are heard in Moscow kitchens, and dissidents demand that the state respect its own Constitution. Suslov's answer is uncompromising: the dissident circles must be broken up, their leaders tried or exiled, and the intelligentsia reminded of its duty. The Party gains calm and order, though the price is paid in creativity and goodwill abroad.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_rewrite_the_history: Since 1956, Soviet history books have been torn between Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin and the uneasy silence that followed his fall. The Pravda article marking Stalin's ninetieth birthday in 1969 showed how far the pendulum has already swung. Suslov's historians can go further, portraying the late leader as the organiser of victory, a creeping rehabilitation that delights the conservatives and alarms the reformers.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_glavlit_offensive: Glavlit, the Main Administration for Safeguarding State Secrets in the Press, decides what Soviet citizens may read. A tighter regime of censorship would strip questionable passages from literary journals, keep foreign publications out of libraries and silence the liberal editors of Novy Mir for good. Hostile voices will find it harder to reach Soviet readers, although scientists will also lose access to useful works from the West.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_closed_society: Detente has brought Western tourists, journalists, jeans and records into the Soviet Union, and with them dangerous ideas. Suslov insists that peaceful coexistence between states does not mean coexistence between ideologies. Fewer exit visas, fewer exchanges and closer supervision of foreigners would seal Soviet society against bourgeois influence, even if foreign trading partners come to view the Union with growing suspicion.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_militant_internationalis: From Indochina to the Horn of Africa, the correlation of forces in the world seems to be shifting towards socialism. Suslov argues that the Soviet Union must not merely observe this historic process but actively lead it, sending arms, money and advisers wherever peoples rise against imperialism. Such a course is expensive and will alarm Washington, but history, he insists, is on Moscow's side.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_liberation_movements: The crumbling Portuguese empire, unrest in Ethiopia and the struggle in South Yemen have opened new fronts in the battle against imperialism. The MPLA in Angola and FRELIMO in Mozambique look to Moscow for weapons and training. By supporting these movements systematically, the Soviet Union can win loyal allies in Africa and Arabia before Washington or Beijing does.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_against_eurocommunism: The Italian, French and Spanish communists under Enrico Berlinguer, Georges Marchais and Santiago Carrillo are drifting towards a democratic road to socialism, independent of Moscow and openly critical of its methods. To Suslov this Eurocommunism is nothing but revisionism in new clothes. Condemning it will cost friendship in Rome and Paris, but it will remind every loyal party that the movement has only one centre.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_world_conference: In June 1969 delegations from seventy-five parties gathered in Moscow for the International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties. Suslov wants a new conference on the same model, with the CPSU firmly at its centre and a joint declaration against imperialism and revisionism. Even if some parties stay away, the image of a united movement assembled in the Kremlin is worth the effort.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_moral_incentives: Kosygin's reforms tried to motivate workers with bonuses and enterprise profits, an approach Suslov considers dangerously close to capitalism. He prefers the methods of socialist emulation: boards of honour, red challenge banners, medals and the title of Hero of Socialist Labour. Consciousness rather than money should drive the Soviet worker, though planners fear that productivity will suffer without material rewards.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_against_the_market: Collective farm markets, cooperative workshops and private plots have grown into a grey economy where prices follow supply and demand. To Suslov, every kopeck earned outside the plan is a step towards the restoration of capitalism. Closing down the cooperative sector will please the Party orthodox and restore ideological clarity, even if shoppers find the shelves emptier than before.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_drawing_together_of_: Party theorists already speak of the Soviet people as a new historical community that transcends nationality. Suslov wants to give substance to this formula through sblizhenie, the drawing together of the nations of the Union: more Russian-language teaching, mixed workforces on the great construction sites and a shared Soviet culture. Moscow hopes that national grievances will fade as a common identity takes root.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_marxism_leninism_in_ever: Young Soviet citizens learn their Marxism-Leninism from dry textbooks and recite it without conviction. Suslov orders a thorough overhaul of ideological education, from the Young Pioneers to university courses in scientific communism. New curricula, better-trained teachers and compulsory study circles cost money, but a generation raised in the faith of the Party will not stray towards bourgeois temptations.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_no_gods_in_the_kremlin: Despite decades of atheist propaganda, churches are filling again and some intellectuals look to Orthodoxy for answers the Party cannot give. Suslov intends to renew the campaign of scientific atheism, tighten the grip of the Council for Religious Affairs and close parishes that grow too popular. Believers and monarchist dreamers are pushed back to the margins, though the faithful will not forget.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_polemic_with_beijing: Since the border clashes on the Ussuri in 1969, Moscow and Beijing have exchanged insults in print as fiercely as they once exchanged fire. Mao's China calls the Soviet Union social-imperialist, while Suslov denounces Maoism as a petty-bourgeois deviation. Renewing the polemic in Pravda and across the world movement will rally loyal parties around Moscow, but it pushes any reconciliation with China further away.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_heir_question: Mikhail Suslov was born in 1902, and his health grows weaker every year. The orthodox wing of the Party must decide who will guard the Marxist-Leninist line once the Grey Cardinal is gone. Konstantin Chernenko offers continuity and a steady hand on the apparatus, while Grigory Romanov of Leningrad promises a younger and harder line.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_heir_chernenko: Konstantin Chernenko has spent his career in the Party apparatus, running the General Department of the Central Committee and the flow of paper that keeps the Politburo working. He is no ideologue, but he is reliable, careful and loyal to collective leadership. Naming him heir assures the cadres that nothing will change abruptly when the Grey Cardinal departs.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_heir_romanov: Grigory Romanov rules Leningrad with a firm hand, keeping its factories, shipyards and restless intellectuals in strict order. Younger than the old guard and admired by the defence industry, he represents a harder and more disciplined variant of orthodoxy. Choosing him as heir signals that the Party's conservatives intend to hold power for another generation.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_iron_line_inherits: What if the guardians of orthodoxy decided that collective leadership had grown too soft? The Neo-Stalinist Platform, led by Sergei Trapeznikov, steps forward to claim Suslov's inheritance and govern in the spirit of the old Vozhd. The cult of the Generalissimo is restored, discipline replaces debate, and the CPSU as it existed under Brezhnev becomes a memory.
COLDWAR_SOV_sus_the_orthodox_union: Suslov's work is complete. The Party line is clear, the censors are vigilant and the schools teach Marxism-Leninism without deviation. The Soviet Union stands as a fortress of orthodox socialism, steady and predictable, though critics whisper that it has also become rigid and slow to adapt to a changing world.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_iron_shurik: Alexander Shelepin, known as Iron Shurik, has led the Komsomol, the KGB and the Committee of Party-State Control. Brezhnev pushed him aside into the trade unions, but now the former Chekist stands at the head of the Party. He promises to restore order, discipline and honesty to a system grown complacent, and the comfortable nomenklatura has every reason to fear him.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_komsomoltsy: Shelepin's power has always rested on a network of former Komsomol leaders: Nikolai Yegorychev of the Moscow party organisation, Nikolai Mesyatsev of state television and Vadim Tikunov of the police ministry. Brezhnev has scattered them to embassies and minor posts. Recalling the Komsomoltsy to Moscow gives the new General Secretary loyal men in key positions, but the established cadres see a rival clan taking their places.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_semichastny_returns: Vladimir Semichastny succeeded Shelepin as chairman of the KGB in 1961 and lost the post in 1967 after Stalin's daughter defected to the West. Since then he has been sitting in Kiev as a deputy premier of Ukraine. Bringing him back to Moscow would place a trusted friend over the security organs and sharpen their fight against foreign subversion.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_trade_union_base: Since 1967 Shelepin has chaired the All-Union Central Council of Trade Unions, a post meant to be a political dead end. Instead he has used it to build a following among the millions of workers who depend on the unions for holidays, housing and sanatoriums. As General Secretary he can turn that following into a pillar of his rule.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_labour_question: The Soviet worker is guaranteed a job, but too often he arrives late, leaves early and drinks on shift. Shelepin must decide how to raise productivity: through strict discipline enforced from above, or by giving workers and their unions a greater share in running their factories and their lives. Either way, the relationship between the state and its working class will change.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_labour_discipline: Absenteeism, idleness and theft from the workplace cost the economy dearly every year. Shelepin intends to tighten labour legislation, tie bonuses to attendance and punish shirkers with transfers and fines. Factory directors welcome the firmer hand, but the trade unions he once led will not easily forgive their former chairman for turning against the workers' privileges.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_absenteeism_raids: Militia patrols and volunteer druzhinniki descend on shops, cinemas, barbershops and bathhouses during working hours, demanding to know why able-bodied citizens are not at their posts. The raids are crude and unpopular, but they send a clear message that the working day belongs to the state. Productivity rises, though so does the bill for policing the streets.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_war_on_drunkenness: Vodka is the curse of the Soviet workplace, responsible for accidents, absenteeism and early deaths, yet it is also one of the state's most reliable sources of revenue. Shelepin is prepared to raise prices, limit sales hours and shut down the taverns near factories. Sober workers will produce more, but the budget will feel the loss and many citizens will resent the new restrictions.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_workers_socialism: Shelepin's years at the head of the trade unions have taught him that workers want respect as well as wages. He proposes a socialism that places the working class at the centre: more say for labour collectives, a greater share of resources for social needs and an end to the arrogance of managers. The unions rally behind him, and talk of free workers' councils begins to spread.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_union_councils: Factory trade union committees already manage holiday vouchers, kindergartens and housing queues, but they have little influence over production. Shelepin wants union councils at every level to take a real part in decisions on working conditions, safety and the distribution of social funds. Workers feel more secure and more valued, though the expanded welfare system will strain the budget.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_workers_control: Lenin dreamed of workers' control over production, and Shelepin himself led the Committee of Party-State Control under Khrushchev. Reviving that spirit, commissions elected by labour collectives would inspect warehouses, audit accounts and expose managers who steal or falsify their reports. Corruption retreats, but the branch ministries resent ordinary workers poking into their affairs.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_order_in_the_streets: Hooliganism, petty crime and public drunkenness have grown in Soviet cities, and citizens complain that the militia does too little. Shelepin promises firm order: more patrols, more volunteer squads and swift punishment for offenders. A country that sees a policeman on every corner feels safer, even if the price of order is paid in watchfulness and fear.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_war_on_corruption: Under Brezhnev's policy of stability of cadres, regional bosses have grown rich on bribes, blat and falsified plan reports. Shelepin intends to unleash the procurators and control commissions against them, from district committees to republican ministries. Honest citizens applaud, but the nomenklatura recognises the threat to its comfortable existence and closes ranks.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_purge_the_brezhnevites: Brezhnev's men still occupy the Central Committee, the ministries and the republican party leaderships: the Dnepropetrovsk clan, the Moldavian circle and their many clients. Shelepin is ready to break them, dismissing the corrupt and retiring the old. Ending the stability of cadres will shake the apparatus to its core, but it will leave the General Secretary master of the Party.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_youth_brigades: The Komsomol has always sent its young volunteers to the great building sites of the Union, from the Virgin Lands to the Siberian hydroelectric dams. Shelepin, who once led the youth league, wants to expand these brigades into a permanent army of young enthusiasts. New towns and factories rise faster, and thousands of young men gain discipline before they enter the armed forces.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_komsomol_economy: Projects like the Baikal-Amur Mainline, planned as a great Komsomol shock construction across the taiga, show what young volunteers can achieve. Shelepin wants the Komsomol to take on a far larger share of such infrastructure work, from roads and railways to power lines. The work is hard and the conditions harsh, but the country gains infrastructure at a fraction of the usual cost.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_foreign_line: Shelepin is a hardliner at home, but where should he turn abroad? Some believe he could heal the rift with Beijing, where he is remembered as a man with whom one can talk. Others expect him to confront the West directly, abandoning the compromises of detente. The General Secretary must choose which front matters most to the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_talk_to_beijing: In the Chinese capital, Shelepin is regarded as a disciplined revolutionary rather than a revisionist bureaucrat. He proposes direct talks between the two camps of the pure line, setting aside years of polemics and border clashes. Whether Mao's China accepts the offer is uncertain, but even an opening would transform the balance of power in Asia.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_confront_the_west: Detente, in Shelepin's eyes, has only allowed the imperialists to buy time and spread their influence into the socialist camp. He prefers a harder course: no concessions on human rights, no compromises over Berlin and a firm answer to every American provocation. The armed forces and the patriotic public welcome the new resolve, although the risk of confrontation grows.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_final_question: Shelepin has reshaped the Party, the trade unions and the security organs, but one question remains: what form should his power take? He could rule openly as a leader standing above the Party, or he could bind his order to the collective leadership and prepare a successor who will carry it forward after him.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_leader_state: What if Shelepin decided that collective leadership was itself the problem? With the Komsomol Vanguard as the new ruling force, Iron Shurik would govern as a Vozhd, a leader whose authority rests on discipline, youth and loyalty rather than on the Central Committee. The old CPSU fades into the background, and the Soviet Union enters an era of personal rule.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_collective_discipline: Instead of ruling alone, Shelepin chooses to embed his reforms in the collective leadership of the Politburo. Discipline becomes the shared creed of the leadership, and Yuri Andropov, the most disciplined of them all, is named the man to carry the work forward. The Party regains its confidence, and the order Shelepin built is meant to outlast him.
COLDWAR_SOV_she_the_iron_order: Shelepin's campaigns have transformed Soviet life. Factories run on schedule, officials fear the inspectors and the streets are quieter than they have been in years. The Iron Order brings stability and productivity to a Union that had grown lax, although scientists and artists complain that little room is left for creativity and free thought.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_chekist_takes_power: For years Yuri Andropov has led the KGB, gathering information on every corner of Soviet society and on all of its failures. Now the former chairman of state security stands at the head of the Party. Austere, intelligent and well informed, he knows that the system is ailing and intends to cure it with discipline, honesty and carefully measured reform.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_kgb_men_in_the_kremlin: Andropov trusts the men he worked with at the Lubyanka. Viktor Chebrikov takes over the KGB, Vladimir Kryuchkov runs foreign intelligence, and Heydar Aliyev, a KGB general who rose to lead Azerbaijan, is brought to Moscow. The security services gain unprecedented influence over the state, and their intelligence networks reach deeper into every institution of the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_young_reformers: Andropov surrounds himself with younger, energetic men: Mikhail Gorbachev, the party chief from Stavropol, Nikolai Ryzhkov, the industrial manager from Uralmash, and Yegor Ligachev, the incorruptible first secretary of Tomsk. They are loyal communists, but they share the conviction that the economy needs fundamental change. Their rise brings fresh ideas to the leadership and tilts the Politburo towards reform.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_lessons_of_budapest: As Soviet ambassador in Budapest in 1956, Andropov watched a socialist state collapse within days and helped crush the uprising that followed. He learned that discontent must be addressed before it explodes, but he also saw how Janos Kadar later rebuilt Hungary with his goulash communism. The Hungarian experience offers lessons in both firmness and flexibility.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_discipline_campaign: Andropov's first great initiative is a campaign against idleness, drunkenness and absenteeism. Militia patrols raid cinemas, shops and bathhouses during working hours, demanding papers from anyone who should be at work. Citizens grumble, but productivity rises, and the KGB gains new authority to investigate even the most powerful officials in the republics.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_road: Andropov knows the Soviet system is in trouble, but his diagnosis allows two cures. He can combine discipline with cautious economic reform, giving managers more independence and the young reformers more influence. Or he can build a Chekist state in which security, control and ideological vigilance hold the Union together. The choice will shape the Soviet future for years to come.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_order_and_reform: Discipline alone cannot save the Soviet economy. Andropov openly admits that the Party does not truly know the society it governs, and he commissions studies on how to give enterprises more independence and workers more responsibility. Order and reform must go hand in hand, and the reformers of the Politburo find themselves listened to at last.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_large_scale_experime: Andropov launches a bold test of economic reform. Enterprises in five industrial ministries, two all-Union and three republican, are allowed to plan more of their own output, keep part of their profits and reward workers for fulfilled delivery contracts. If the large-scale experiment succeeds, its methods could be extended across the entire Soviet economy.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_economic_department: The Central Committee has never had a department responsible for the economy as a whole, only branch departments that defend their own industries. Andropov creates one and places Nikolai Ryzhkov, former director of the Uralmash works, at its head. With a single team studying the economy, the Party can finally plan reforms rather than simply issue targets.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_technology_gap: KGB reports leave no doubt: the Soviet Union is falling behind the West in computers and microelectronics, and the gap grows wider every year. Copying Western designs and smuggling components through third countries can only go so far. Andropov orders a crash programme to build a native computing industry before the technological lag becomes a strategic one.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_chekist_state: Andropov concludes that only the security organs remain uncorrupted enough to hold the Union together. The KGB receives wider powers over the economy, the Party and the media, and its officers are placed in key positions across the state. Order is restored and enemies are watched closely, but scientists and intellectuals sense the air growing heavier.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_gorky_for_sakharov: Andrei Sakharov, father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, has become the most prominent voice of the human rights movement. Rather than put him on trial, the KGB proposes to exile him to Gorky, a city closed to foreigners, where he can be watched and silenced. The dissident movement loses its figurehead, though Washington and the Western press will protest loudly.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_kgb_economy: Speculators, black-market traders and officials who live far beyond their salaries have built a shadow economy of their own. Andropov sets the KGB on their trail, from the trade networks of Moscow to the fish shops of the Okean affair. Unearned incomes are confiscated, and the nomenklatura learns that its privileges no longer guarantee protection.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_informant_society: Every workplace, apartment block and research institute already has its watchers, but Andropov wants a denser network still. New informants are recruited among students, engineers and pensioners, and reports flow to the regional KGB directorates in unprecedented numbers. Foreign intelligence services find it harder to operate, but citizens learn to guard their words more carefully than ever.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_cotton_affair_expose: For years the Uzbek SSR has reported cotton harvests that never existed, and Moscow has paid enormous sums for phantom fibre. Under Sharaf Rashidov, the republic's leaders built a vast system of bribery and falsified reports. Andropov sends investigators to Tashkent to expose the pripiski, punish the guilty and remind every republic that the centre is watching.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_shchelokov_purge: Nikolai Shchelokov, Brezhnev's old friend and Minister of Internal Affairs since the late 1960s, has turned the militia into his personal domain, riddled with corruption and luxury. Andropov removes him and sends KGB officers to purge the ministry from top to bottom. The militia becomes cleaner and cheaper to run, while Brezhnev's old circle loses one of its most powerful members.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_a_way_out_of_afghanistan: Andropov knows how easily a limited intervention becomes an endless war. Wherever Soviet soldiers are bogged down, as they could be in the mountains of Afghanistan, he prefers a dignified way out through negotiations rather than further escalation. Easing such burdens would calm tensions with the West and let the Union concentrate on its problems at home.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_talks_with_beijing: Years of Sino-Soviet hostility have brought nothing but border garrisons and wasted resources. Andropov proposes to resume regular consultations with Beijing at the level of deputy foreign ministers, without preconditions. The Chinese leadership will decide whether to respond, but any thaw would ease the burden on the Far East and weaken American influence in Asia.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_succession: Andropov's kidneys are failing, and he spends more and more time connected to a dialysis machine at the Kremlin hospital in Kuntsevo. The Politburo receives his instructions in writing while rumours spread through Moscow. Before his illness ends his rule, the General Secretary must decide who will carry his work forward: a reformer, a guardian of continuity or a fellow Chekist.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_heir_gorbachev: Mikhail Gorbachev, the energetic party leader from Stavropol, is Andropov's protege and the youngest man in the leadership. Open to new ideas, he has already taken charge of agriculture and much of the economic agenda. Naming him heir tells the Party that the reforms will continue, and it alarms the old guard who would prefer a calmer succession.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_heir_chernenko: The elderly members of the Politburo do not want another reformer, and they rally around Konstantin Chernenko, Brezhnev's faithful chief of staff. His health is poor and his ideas are few, but he guarantees that no one will lose his post. Choosing him satisfies the cadres and preserves stability, even if the reforms quietly lose their momentum.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_heir_aliyev: Heydar Aliyev rose through the ranks of the Azerbaijani KGB, has led his republic's Communist Party since 1969 and is Andropov's choice for First Deputy Premier in Moscow. As a Muslim from the Caucasus at the summit of Soviet power, he would show the peoples of the Union that the Kremlin belongs to them all. To the KGB, he is simply one of their own.
COLDWAR_SOV_and_the_disciplined_union: Andropov's campaigns have left their mark. Officials think twice before taking bribes, workers arrive on time, and the Party has regained some of the authority it lost in the years of stagnation. The Disciplined Union is not yet a reformed one, but it has gained the strength and confidence to face the challenges of the coming decade.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_marshals_hour: Since Marshal Zhukov was ousted in 1957, the army has been kept away from the summit of power. Now Marshal Andrei Grechko, Minister of Defence and a veteran of the battles for the Caucasus and Kiev, stands at the head of the Party. There is no coup and no junta, only a soldier in the General Secretary's chair, and the armed forces finally have a voice at the top.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_general_staff_in_the: The Chief of the General Staff has always carried out the decisions of the political leadership without taking part in them. Grechko gives Viktor Kulikov, and after him Nikolai Ogarkov, a regular voice in the Politburo's deliberations. Military planning becomes faster and better coordinated with the needs of the state, and the General Staff becomes the brain of the Union as well as of the army.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_yepishevs_political_dire: General Alexei Yepishev heads the Main Political Directorate of the Soviet Army and Navy, responsible for the ideological education of every soldier and sailor. His political officers are both a link between the Party and the barracks and a guarantee of loyalty. Strengthening the directorate raises the morale of the troops and reassures the Party cadres that the army remains firmly under their control.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_defence_council: The Defence Council of the USSR brings together the General Secretary, the Minister of Defence, the Chief of the General Staff and the leaders of the defence industry. Under Grechko it becomes the true centre of power, deciding not only military questions but also economic priorities. Decisions are swift and clear, though the civilians of the Politburo feel increasingly sidelined.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_doctrine: Soviet military thinkers have long debated whether the next war will be decided by armoured masses or by strategic missiles. Grechko himself trusts in tank armies and trained reserves, but the rocket designers and the Strategic Rocket Forces argue that nuclear power is the only true guarantee of security. The General Secretary must decide where the Union's resources will go.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_mass_army: Grechko's war was won by millions of soldiers and tens of thousands of tanks, and he sees no reason to change the formula. Conscription is enforced more strictly, reserve divisions are filled and training for reservists is expanded. The Soviet Army becomes larger and harder to defeat in defence, although the economy loses more young men to the barracks.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_tank_armies_of_the_w: The Group of Soviet Forces in Germany is the spearhead of the Warsaw Pact, with five armies poised along the inner German border. Grechko wants them equipped with the newest tanks, the T-64 and the coming T-72, and trained for a rapid thrust to the Rhine. NATO planners watch nervously as the breakthrough power of Soviet armour grows.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_mobilisation_reserves: In the event of war, the Soviet Union must be able to call millions of reservists to the colours within days. Grechko orders mobilisation plans revised, depots stocked and military commissariats modernised in every district. The effort fills warehouses with equipment and supplies that could otherwise reach the shops, but the Union will never again be caught unprepared as in 1941.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_nuclear_shield: Marshal Grechko is persuaded that the decisive weapon of the age is the intercontinental ballistic missile. New generations of heavy rockets, among them the R-36M known in the West as the SS-18, will give the Strategic Rocket Forces the power to deter any aggressor. Behind such a shield, Soviet diplomats can negotiate from a position of strength.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_strategic_triad: Missiles in silos can be targeted, but submarines hiding in the Barents Sea and bombers on airborne alert are far harder to destroy. Grechko orders the development of all three legs of the strategic triad, from new Delta-class missile submarines to modern long-range bombers. The investment is enormous, and Washington will see it as another escalation of the arms race.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_against_salt: The SALT negotiations promise to limit the strategic arsenals of both superpowers, but many officers believe they would freeze Soviet missile forces just as they are catching up. Grechko lends his weight to the sceptics in the Politburo and the defence industry, arguing that no agreement can replace real military strength. Detente cools, and the arms race continues unchecked.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_far_eastern_command: Since the clashes with China in 1969, dozens of Soviet divisions have been stationed along the Amur and the Ussuri, yet coordinating them from Moscow is slow and inefficient. Grechko proposes a separate high command for the Far East, headquartered in Ulan-Ude, with its own air bases and reserves, to defend Soviet territory against any threat from China or Japan.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_suvorov_schools: Founded during the Great Patriotic War to educate the orphans of fallen soldiers, the Suvorov and Nakhimov schools have become the cradle of the Soviet officer corps. Grechko wants more of them, with better teachers and stricter standards, to produce cadets who are ready to command. The armed forces will gain officers who have worn the uniform since childhood.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_school_of_the_nation: Every year young men from all fifteen republics enter the Soviet Army, many of them speaking little Russian. Grechko sees military service as the great melting pot of the Union, where Uzbeks, Lithuanians and Russians learn a common language of command and a shared Soviet identity. The barracks become a school of friendship between peoples and of loyalty to the Union.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_arms_for_allies: Soviet weapons have become the most effective form of diplomacy, from Kalashnikovs in Africa to MiG fighters in the Middle East. Grechko wants arms exports organised on a larger scale, with long-term credits for friendly regimes and cheaper aid packages for liberation movements. The defence industry gains new markets, and every rifle shipped abroad buys influence for Moscow.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_military_advisers: In Egypt, thousands of Soviet advisers and air-defence crews helped rebuild the army after the defeat of 1967. Grechko proposes to expand such missions in Egypt and extend them to Syria and Iraq, offering training, staff work and modern doctrine to friendly armies. It is up to Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad to accept, but every adviser they welcome draws them closer to Moscow.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_heir_of_the_marshal: Grechko has passed seventy, and even a marshal's health cannot last forever. The question of succession weighs on the leadership: should another man close to the armed forces continue the course, or should power return to the civilian Party apparatus? The decision will determine whether the army's hour becomes an era or merely an episode.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_heir_ustinov: Dmitry Ustinov has directed the Soviet defence industry since he became People's Commissar for Armaments in 1941. Though not a career soldier, he knows every design bureau and every factory of the military-industrial complex. Naming him heir assures the defence industry that its privileged position will survive the Marshal, and that the armed forces will keep receiving the best the Union can produce.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_return_to_civilian_rule: The Marshal's leadership has strengthened the armed forces, but many in the Party fear that the generals are growing too powerful. Grechko himself accepts that the army should step back once his task is done. Konstantin Chernenko, a quiet man of the Party apparatus, is named heir, reassuring the cadres that the Party will once again command the gun.
COLDWAR_SOV_gre_the_council_of_marshals: What if the marshals decided that the Party had failed the Union? The Council of Marshals takes power, stripping the Central Committee of its authority and placing the country under the direct rule of the High Command. Grechko becomes head of a military government, promising order and strength. Many citizens accept the change in silence, but the shock to the old system is immense.
